newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: EU ponder fallout from French election.
newsitem.headline: EU ponder fallout from French election.

text.p: European Union foreign ministers reacted cautiously on Monday to a sweeping French Socialist election victory that has raised the spectre of a delay to a new EU treaty and plans for a single currency.

At a routine ministerial meeting in Luxembourg to discuss the treaty, due to be agreed at an EU summit in Amsterdam in two weeks, most ministers said they wanted to wait and see what Sunday's stunning triumph by the French left would bring.
"It's too early to say," British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook said as he arrived for the meeting.
But Germany's Klaus Kinkel aggressively sought to play down the chances of a radical change in French policy.

"The realities of power will push things in the same direction as they have been," Kinkel told reporters. "I think the economic austerity course will stay as far as the main points are concerned. (But) there will be nuances."
The French Socialists have said they are committed to monetary union, but with conditions, including a flexible interpretation of the Maastricht treaty.

They want Italy and Spain to be in the first wave of countries to adopt the single currency from 1999 and have made clear they are unwilling to continue the fiscal austerity policy conducted by the outgoing government to qualify France for EMU.
Although this -- and a crisis over proposed German accounting methods -- have led to renewed discussion of a delay in EMU, most ministers were low key in their comments.
Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini said the election of the Socialists marked an important change but that the rest of the EU would have to wait to see what it meant for Paris's European policy.
"It depends who will be foreign minister," Dutch Foreign Minister Hans Van Mierlo told reporters. The Netherlands currently holds the EU presidency.
Most said there was no reason that a new EU treaty could not still be agreed at Amsterdam on June 16 and 17 despite the French turnaround.

Kinkel said the Franco-German alliance, which in the past has often led the EU and been the driving force behind treaty chances, would remain intact because the two countries were "emotionally and rationally the closest partners".

Diplomats said, however, that the election result meant no progress on the new treaty would be made at the Luxembourg meeting -- leaving very little time for the hardest issues to be sorted out before the summit.
